intros.market: Five CAs control 88% of trusted certificate issuance. ISRG leads at 32%, followed by Google Trust Services at 21.1% and DigiCert at 17.8%. The remaining 74 CAs in the tail collectively hold just 12% market share, creating a system where operational failure at any top-3 provider would affect over two-thirds of the web.
intros.trust: 335 roots are distributed across four trust stores, but only 90 roots appear in all four programs and only 38 CA owners achieve universal inclusion. Microsoft maintains 142 roots not present in Chrome, Mozilla, or Apple, creating a fragmentation problem where certificate chains valid in Edge may fail elsewhere. This disagreement across stores forces CAs to maintain multiple hierarchies and complicates incident response when a root's trustworthiness is questioned in one program but not others.
intros.conc: The market HHI of 1980 indicates high concentration approaching the 2500 threshold that economists consider a monopolistic structure. CR3 concentration of 70.9% means three organizations control nearly three-quarters of all issuance. This systemic dependency means a prolonged outage or compromise at ISRG, Google, or DigiCert would immediately affect the majority of HTTPS connections globally.
intros.tail: 74 CAs operate in the long tail with minimal issuance but full trust store inclusion, creating asymmetric risk. Each holds the same cryptographic authority as high-volume providers despite serving niche markets or single-organization use cases. The incidents data shows 55 CAs have disclosed problems, meaning many tail CAs have operational track records invisible in their market share.
intros.geo: 92.7% of trusted certificate issuance originates from CAs incorporated in the United States, issued by just 15 organizations. Europe hosts 44 CAs but represents only 7.2% of issuance, while 17 Asia-Pacific CAs collectively account for 0.09%. This geographic concentration mirrors the market concentration, with both pointing to systemic dependency on a small number of US-based entities.
intros.gov: 30 government-operated or state-owned CAs hold positions in public trust stores but represent only 0.09% of issuance. These entities span regions with varying legal frameworks and accountability structures. Their presence creates jurisdiction risk beyond their issuance volume, as state control introduces compelled access and surveillance considerations distinct from commercial CA governance.
intros.jurisdiction: Five jurisdictions are classified as high legal risk for compelled disclosure or surveillance: China, Russia, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Hong Kong. India and Turkey are assessed as moderate risk. CAs incorporated in these regions operate under legal frameworks that may compel certificate issuance, key access, or disclosure without judicial oversight, creating scenarios where browser trust becomes a vector for state surveillance.
intros.ops: 1800 incidents across 55 CAs have been disclosed since tracking began, with misissuance (684) and governance failures (595) as leading categories. Only 33% of incidents are self-detected, while 17% come from external researchers and just 7% from audits. Policy failures account for 265 incidents and disclosure failures for 167, indicating systematic weakness in both operational controls and transparency obligations.
intros.crypto: Root certificate algorithms and key sizes vary across the 335 trusted roots, with aging cryptographic postures creating upgrade dependencies. The BR readiness data shows CAs must navigate compatibility constraints while preparing for future post-quantum transitions. Standards compliance intersects with the 6657 total obligations tracked in the regulatory surface, where cryptographic requirements are scattered across multiple overlapping frameworks.
intros.distrust: 16 distrust events have occurred across all browser programs, with 14 attributed to compliance or operational failure and 10 following a pattern of repeated issues. 7 events involved negligent noncompliance, 3 demonstrated incompetence, and 3 involved willful circumvention of requirements. The median runway from distrust announcement to enforcement is 1185 days, though this varies significantly by root program and severity.
intros.policy: 35 active TLS CAs face cascading certificate validity reductions under SC-081, with 5 not yet ready for the 100-day limit arriving in March 2027 and only 9 demonstrating readiness for the 47-day requirement in March 2029. The compliance burden underlying this transition has grown 121-fold since 2000 to 6657 total obligations, 76% of which are mandatory requirements. Zero ballots have passed since 2022 to address this complexity, leaving CAs to navigate a regulatory surface that expands faster than their median 62-day certificate lifetimes.
intros.governance: Root program oversight coverage has collapsed from 67.8% (Chrome) and 78% (Mozilla) in 2019 to 18.4% and 9.9% respectively in 2025, even as 223 incidents occurred. Microsoft provides zero formal oversight despite maintaining a unique trust store with 142 exclusive roots. Chrome and Mozilla have collectively commented on 1564 oversight bugs and 548 substantive matters, but their declining coverage rates mean most incidents now proceed without program intervention until external researchers surface them.
intros.community: 56 organizations are CA/B Forum members but only 21 actively participate, with 35 contributing zero ballot activity. Stephen Davidson of Sectigo has proposed 36 ballots and endorsed 1, dominating individual participation. This concentration of governance work in a small minority mirrors the market concentration at 88%, where a handful of entities shape both issuance and policy while the majority remain silent on decisions affecting the entire ecosystem.
intros.audit: Auditors detected just 28% of the 432 in-scope incidents that occurred during the periods their letters covered, meaning 312 real operational failures coexisted with clean audit opinions. 39 CAs show high transparency gaps between audit letter scope and incident disclosure history, while 7 letters contain qualified opinions signaling identified weaknesses. 63.8% of WebTrust findings and 70.8% of ETSI findings are self-reported by CAs rather than discovered by auditors, indicating audit surveillance serves primarily as a documentation exercise rather than independent verification.
